introduction.heading: What is Node.js?
introduction.description: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine that lets you run JavaScript outside the browser - on servers, in command-line tools, and anywhere else you need it. It's non-blocking and event-driven by design, which makes it a natural fit for servers and tools that spend a lot of time waiting on I/O: network requests, file reads, database queries.

runtime.heading: The Event Loop
runtime.description: Node.js runs your JavaScript on a single thread, but it doesn't sit idle waiting on slow work like a file read or a network request. It hands that work off and keeps going, then comes back to run callbacks, resolved promises, and timers once they're ready. The order it runs them in - synchronous code, then microtasks, then macrotasks like setTimeout - is the event loop.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: Install Node.js from nodejs.org, or manage versions with nvm
Run a file directly with node app.js - no build step required
Run npm init to create a package.json for your project
Install packages with npm install <package> and require or import them
Reach for built-in modules like fs, http, and path before installing a package for the job

fullExample.description: This example ties together the core concepts above in one realistic file. Click through the steps to see which lines each one is talking about.

steps.label: Require a built-in module
steps.explanation: require("http") pulls in one of Node's built-in modules - it ships with Node itself, so there's nothing to install.

steps.label: Keep state in memory
steps.explanation: A top-level variable lives for as long as the process runs, and is shared by every request this same server instance handles.

steps.label: Create the server
steps.explanation: createServer takes a callback that Node invokes once for every incoming request, handing it a request object to read and a response object to write to.

steps.label: Handle a GET request
steps.explanation: writeHead sets the status code and headers, then end() sends the body and finishes the response.

steps.label: Read a POST body as a stream
steps.explanation: req is a readable stream, not a ready-made string - the body arrives in chunks, so you listen for "data" events and concatenate them yourself.

steps.label: Act once the stream ends
steps.explanation: The "end" event fires after the last chunk arrives - only then is it safe to parse the full body and respond.

steps.label: Fall back for unknown routes
steps.explanation: Any request that didn't match an earlier branch falls through to this default 404 response.

steps.label: Start listening
steps.explanation: listen(port, callback) hands control to Node's event loop. The callback runs once, when the server is ready to accept connections, and the process then stays alive waiting for requests.

steps.label: Export for reuse
steps.explanation: module.exports makes this file's server importable elsewhere with require("./server") - the same require() from step 1, now pointing at your own file instead of a built-in.
